section.heading: Average Value of a Function
section.paragraph: The average value of a function over an interval provides us with an application of the definite integral. Recall that the average value of a set of $$n$$ numbers $$y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}$$ is the number

Now, suppose $$f$$ is a continuous function defined on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Let’s divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal length $$(b - a) \slash n$$ . Choose points $$x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}$$ in the first, second, …, $$n$$ th subintervals, respectively. Then, the average value of the numbers $$f\left( x_{1} \right),f\left( x_{2} \right),\ldots,f\left( x_{n} \right)$$ , given by
$$\frac{f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + \ldots + f\left( x_{n} \right)}{n}$$
is an approximation of the average of all the values of $$f(x)$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . This expression can be written in the form

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{b - a}{b - a}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} + f\left( x_{2} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} + \ldots + f\left( x_{n} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n}} \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{b - a}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right) \cdot \frac{b - a}{n} + f\left( x_{2} \right) \cdot \frac{b - a}{n} + \ldots + f\left( x_{n} \right) \cdot \frac{b - a}{n}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\frac{b - a}{b - a}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} + f\left( x_{2} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n} + \ldots + f\left( x_{n} \right) \cdot \frac{1}{n}} \right\rbrack} = \frac{1}{b - a}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right)\Delta x + f\left( x_{2} \right)\Delta x + \ldots + f\left( x_{n} \right)\Delta x} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$

As $$n$$ gets larger and larger, the expression (12) approximates the average value of $$f(x)$$ over $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ with increasing accuracy. But the sum inside the brackets in (12) is a Riemann sum of the function $$f$$ over $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . In view of this, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( x_{n} \right)}{n} \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{b - a}\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack {f\left( x_{1} \right)\Delta x + f\left( x_{2} \right)\Delta x + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( x_{n} \right)\Delta x} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left\lbrack \frac{f\left( x_{1} \right) + f\left( x_{2} \right) + \cdot \cdot \cdot + f\left( x_{n} \right)}{n} \right\rbrack} = \frac{1}{b - a}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: We now give a geometric interpretation of the average value of a function $$f$$ over an interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . Suppose $$f(x)$$ is nonnegative, so that the definite integral

gives the area under the graph of $$f$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ (Figure 26). Observe that, in general, the “height” $$f(x)$$ varies from point to point. Can we replace $$f(x)$$ by a constant function $$g(x) = k$$ (which has constant height) such that the areas under each of the two functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ are the same? If so, since the area under the graph of $$g$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ is $$k\left( {b - a} \right)$$ we have
$$\begin{array}{rll} {k\left( {b - a} \right)} & = & {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}} \\ k & = & {\frac{1}{b - a}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}} \end{array}$$

so $$k$$ is the average value of $$f$$ over [ $$a$$ , $$b$$ ]. Thus, the average value of a function $$f$$ over an interval [ $$a$$ , $$b$$ ] is the height of a rectangle with base of length $$(b - a)$$ that has the same area as that of the region under the graph of $$f$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = b$$ .
